Demand Forecasting with Historical Features¶

Author: Mohammed Adeen Shaik

Research question¶

Does gradient boosting improve demand error over a seasonal baseline in chronological evaluation?

Data and evidence¶

UCI Bike Sharing data, used as a demand-planning teaching example.

Fresh execution on 11 October 2026 using the committed pipeline and random seed 42. Validation selected gradient_boosting. On 2,582 later-period rows, selected-model MAE was 32.19 and seasonal-naive MAE was 85.74, a 62.5% reduction. This is rolling one-step evaluation using observed prior targets, not an advance multi-step forecast.

Measure Value
selected model gradient_boosting
seasonal lag 168
train rows 12047
validation rows 2582
test rows 2582
random seed 42
Test model MAE RMSE sMAPE
test_gradient_boosting 32.19 51.45 0.221
test_seasonal_naive 85.74 149.41 0.456
test_selected 32.19 51.45 0.221

Reading guide¶

Read each explanation before its code cell. Run from top to bottom in the documented working directory. A saved chart is an output snapshot, not proof that this notebook was rerun today. The final section collects findings and visual evidence.

Method¶

Earlier periods train the model, the next period selects it and the last period measures error. Lag and rolling statistics use earlier observed targets.

Interpretation limits¶

This is rolling one-step evaluation with observed history, not a multi-step forecast from a single origin. Weather variables may be observed rather than known in advance. Row-based lags can differ from calendar-hour lags when timestamps are missing. Bike rentals are not actual retail SKU sales.

Demand Forecast — Error Analysis¶

Run the training pipeline first. This notebook compares the selected forecast with the seasonal baseline and examines error concentration.

plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False, "font.size": 11})

Guide to code step 2¶

Load the source table. A DataFrame is a spreadsheet-like table in memory. The path must point to the documented input file; loading a file does not validate its contents.

from pathlib import Path
import json
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd

ARTIFACTS = Path("../reports/results")
forecasts = pd.read_csv(ARTIFACTS / "test_forecasts.csv", parse_dates=["timestamp"])
metrics = json.loads((ARTIFACTS / "metrics.json").read_text())
metrics

Guide to code step 3¶

Read the chart. The axis labels identify units and the grouping defines what is compared. A visual association does not establish cause. Rate charts need denominators; truncated axes can exaggerate small differences.

tail = forecasts.tail(24 * 14)
figure, axis = plt.subplots(figsize=(13, 5))
axis.plot(tail["timestamp"], tail["actual"], label="Actual", color="#0F172A")
axis.plot(tail["timestamp"], tail["selected_forecast"], label="Selected forecast", color="#2563EB")
axis.set(title="Latest Two Weeks of Held-out Demand", ylabel="Demand")
axis.legend()
axis.grid(alpha=0.25)
figure.autofmt_xdate()
figure.tight_layout()

Guide to code step 4¶

Summarize observations. Grouping collects rows with the same label. Counts and sums produce totals; a mean of a binary 0/1 indicator gives a rate. Always identify the denominator and keep missing categories visible.

Read the chart. The axis labels identify units and the grouping defines what is compared. A visual association does not establish cause. Rate charts need denominators; truncated axes can exaggerate small differences.

forecasts["absolute_error"] = (forecasts["actual"] - forecasts["selected_forecast"]).abs()
forecasts["hour"] = forecasts["timestamp"].dt.hour
hourly = forecasts.groupby("hour", as_index=False)["absolute_error"].mean()
figure, axis = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 5))
axis.bar(hourly["hour"], hourly["absolute_error"], color="#7C3AED")
axis.set(title="Mean Absolute Error by Hour", xlabel="Hour", ylabel="MAE")
figure.tight_layout()
